2026 Paris Motor Show • 2027 Hyundai Bayon Finally Looks More Like a Box and Less Like an Egg
12 New Hot Wheels Red Line Club Models and a Super Treasure Hunt You Didn’t Know About
17 photos
Photo: Hot Wheels Malaysia
I didn’t even go to the 40th Annual Hot Wheels Collectors Convention in Los Angeles and I’m still trying to recover from it. That’s because Mattel’s official sneak peeks for November, December and the first part of 2027 are slightly overwhelming.
I’ve already gone through most of them in my two previous stories, covering the basic and the premium models. And I’ve saved the Red Line Club special items for last. Before we talk about them, I also wanted to show you what the next Super Treasure Hunt for next year will be: the Porsche 911 Carrera T! You’ll see it pictured with no wheels, featuring a Spectraflame Red finish and some white lines for contrast.
It will be the fourth variation for this casting, and the third Porsche STH in a row after the 911 Carrera RS 2.7 (2026), the 911 Rallye (2025). If you’re a fan of the German manufacturer, you may already know the premium 911 GT3 RS will be a Chase item next year. But wait, there’s more! We still have some RLC news to look at. The Datsun 240Z will be continuing the Chase trend, and it’s coming this fall.
Phil Riehlman’s Z is one of the castings that can move between different series with ease, despite the obvious inconvenience: it doesn’t have any opening features. It hasn’t been an RLC exclusive since 2018, when only 6,500 units left the factory.
The new Chase Z won’t be as rare as the 2013 HWC.com Special Edition version (3,500 units) or the 31st Annual Hot Wheels Collectors Convention Dinner Car (1,600 units). Only time will tell what its market value will look like, though.
Photo: Hot Wheels Malaysia You may have seen photos of the VW T1 Rockster that’s also on its way. I almost can’t understand why this casting isn’t more popular. It might be because it’s too extreme compared to the regular vans, even though those were 1/4-mile monsters to begin with.
The 2023 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon 170 is a new model for Mattel, and I’m “dying” to see the engine bay. It’s bound to be at least one step above the '18 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon, which Brendon Vetuskey was also responsible for.
The RLC Demon will use brand-new Modern Drag Real Riders wheels, which might trickle down into the Car Culture or Boulevard series later down the road. Is this yet another sign that Dragstrip Demons will be returning in 2027, or is that simply wishful thinking on my behalf? The second iteration of the 1969 Ferrari 312 P isn’t identical to the first one although I might seem like that from afar.
It has a new race number on, and new Italian Classic Exotic Real Riders wheels plus it’s inside a blister card and not in a big black box like the first time around. I assume a new variation of the Ferrari 499P Modificata could be in development, too, as it makes no sense for the manufacturer to just release one version of a casting and then simply forget about it. Will it be yellow?
Photo: Lamley Group The 1995 BMW M3 E36 is be the new Membership car for next year, marking the return to Germany after two years spent in the USA (1965 Shelby Cobra 427 S/C in 2026) and Japan (1995 Honda Integra Type R in 2025). I’m almost concerned by the wheels it’s rolling on, even though I have no intention of purchasing it when it goes live on Mattel Creations. Can it truly top the impact the Spectraflame bright orange First Edition release had in 2025?
We’ve got two other replicas of German icons on the list for today, and I’m much too young to dream about the 1972 BMW 2002 . Well, I’m also not nearly rich enough to shop for the 1994 Porsche 911 Turbo 3.6 S “Package” either, but the “math” is much easier in the 1/64th-scale Universe. I’m not saying buying this new collectible will be easy, at least if you don’t have an Overdrive account.
But I’m sure there’s still hope of finding one for under $70 on eBay six to 12 months after its release. The opening engine cover might explain the “BLK MGC” license plate, and I can’t believe I’ve driven one of these in the real world thanks to Porsche having extended that invitation. The Custom ‘72 Datsun 240Z has had six iterations thus far, and there are only 10,000 units out there for the 2019 version.
It’s hard to tell if the new one is blue or purple, but we’ve seen both either way. The 1966 Ford GT40 MKIV is yet another Red Line Club vehicle I’d like in my collection. The lettered tires are a bonus this time, and it’s probably safe to assume we’ll see at least two or three more iterations before 2030. I’m surprised to see that the team in El Segundo chose the 1999 Type R to be the next Honda Red Line Club model.
Photo: Lamley Group Promoting it to “Chase” from the get-go almost feels like safety measure meant to bring in more customers. This way the “Sold Out” message might just show up on your screen minutes after the casting’s debut. You could slap a yellow finish onto almost any car and I’d be interested, and seeing it on the 1998 Subaru Impreza WRX STI makes me realize I was wrong to think Mattel could never top the blue version.
Speaking of blue, we finally know what the Ferrari F8 Spider will look like in the Red Line Club series. It doesn’t seem to have any opening parts, so it might as well have been used for the Elite 64 collection instead. I should follow up on my decision to get some BBR Ferraris next!
